newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wants study of Iraqi nerve gas documents.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants study of Iraqi nerve gas documents.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday he asked a commission investigating Gulf War illness to study newly released documents suggesting U.S. troops may have been exposed to Iraqi nerve gas in 1991.

According to a report released by the Defence Department on Tuesday, the Central Intelligence Agency warned the U.S. Army in November 1991 that troops had been involved in the destruction of an Iraqi ammunition dump at Kamisiyah, where the Iraqis said chemical weapons were present.

Clinton told reporters on Wednesday he had written to Dr. Joyce Lashof, the chair of the presidential advisory committee on Gulf War veterans' illnesses, asking the committee to focus on the newly released documents.

"It is essential that we get all the help we can from the (committee) in understanding the full significance of the documents and any other new information that might come to light," Clinton told a news conference. "We cannot stop until we get all the answers about Gulf War illnesses."

A senior Defence Department official, Bernard Rostker, said the CIA informed the Army in November 1991 that troops had apparently been involved in the destruction at Kamisiyah and that the Iraqis said chemical arms were there.

But the Army subsequently misidentified U.S. troops in southern Iraq when the thousands of chemical rockets were destroyed, and U.S. intelligence officials did not believe Iraqi statements about the arms. The investigation was dropped until 1994, the report said.

Rostker stressed there was still no proof that any U.S. troops were exposed to nerve agents from the destruction and that, at any rate, the controversial event did not provide an answer to the mystery of Gulf War illness.

Gulf War troops complained of symptoms ranging from memory loss to muscle aches, and the Pentagon last year notified 20,000 veterans that they may have suffered low-level exposure from blast clouds drifting away from Kamisiyah.
Under orders from Clinton, the Defence Department is conducting an intense investigation of Gulf War illness, although experts concluded no common cause of Gulf medical complaints existed.
